prism-2014-junior-01.title: Compute both
prism-2014-junior-01.body:
50% means half: half of 50 is 25 and half of 40 is 20. The difference is $25 - 20 = 5$.

**Answer: (B) 5**

prism-2014-junior-02.title: Common denominator
prism-2014-junior-02.body:
With denominator 420: $\frac34 = \frac{315}{420}$, $\frac35 = \frac{252}{420}$, $\frac23 = \frac{280}{420}$, $\frac57 = \frac{300}{420}$, $0.7 = \frac{294}{420}$. The largest numerator is 315.

**Answer: (A) $\frac34$**

prism-2014-junior-03.title: Two lists
prism-2014-junior-03.body:
Multiples of 7: 7, 14, 21, 28, 35 (5 numbers). Ending in 7: 7, 17, 27, 37 (4 numbers). The number 7 is on both lists, so the total is $5 + 4 - 1 = 8$.

**Answer: (C) 8**

prism-2014-junior-04.title: Half the day length
prism-2014-junior-04.body:
From 08:04 to 18:38 is 10 hours 34 minutes. Half of that is 5 hours 17 minutes. Adding to sunrise: $08{:}04 + 5{:}17 = 13{:}21$.

**Answer: (C) 13:21**

prism-2014-junior-04.title: Average the times
prism-2014-junior-04.body:
In minutes after midnight, sunrise is $8\times60 + 4 = 484$ and sunset is $18\times60 + 38 = 1118$. The average is $\frac{484 + 1118}{2} = 801$ minutes $= 13$ h $21$ min.

**Answer: (C) 13:21**

prism-2014-junior-05.title: Convert to eggs
prism-2014-junior-05.body:
3 loaves are worth $3\times4 = 12$ eggs. Each chocolate bar is worth 2 eggs, so 12 eggs buy $12\div2 = 6$ bars.

**Answer: (D) 6**

prism-2014-junior-05.title: Loaf in bars
prism-2014-junior-05.body:
Since a bar is 2 eggs, a loaf (4 eggs) is worth 2 bars. So 3 loaves are worth $3\times2 = 6$ bars.

**Answer: (D) 6**

prism-2014-junior-06.title: Too few doesn't work
prism-2014-junior-06.body:
If Peter ate 6 or fewer, the other two would share at least 12, so one of them would have at least 6 — not fewer than Peter. So Peter ate at least 7. And 7 works: the others could have 6 and 5 ($7 + 6 + 5 = 18$).

**Answer: (C) 7**

prism-2014-junior-06.title: Equal shares
prism-2014-junior-06.body:
If all three ate the same they would each have $18\div3 = 6$. Peter must have strictly more than each of the others, so more than the average: at least 7. The split $7, 6, 5$ shows 7 is possible.

**Answer: (C) 7**

prism-2014-junior-07.title: Fill the chairs
prism-2014-junior-07.body:
Any of the 4 people can sit in the first chair, then any of the remaining 3 in the second, 2 in the third and 1 in the last: $4\times3\times2\times1 = 24$.

**Answer: (D) 24**

prism-2014-junior-07.title: Count by who sits first
prism-2014-junior-07.body:
If A sits first, B, C, D can be arranged in the other three chairs in 6 ways (BCD, BDC, CBD, CDB, DBC, DCB). The same is true for each of the 4 people in the first chair: $4\times6 = 24$.

**Answer: (D) 24**

prism-2014-junior-08.title: Count team-games
prism-2014-junior-08.body:
Each of the 10 teams plays 3 games: $10\times3 = 30$ team-appearances. Every game involves two teams, so it is counted twice. The number of games is $30\div2 = 15$.

**Answer: (A) 15**

prism-2014-junior-08.title: Rounds
prism-2014-junior-08.body:
In each “round” where every team plays once, the 10 teams form 5 games. Three such rounds give $3\times5 = 15$ games.

**Answer: (A) 15**

prism-2014-junior-09.title: Factorise
prism-2014-junior-09.body:
$62500 = 625\times100 = 25\times25\times10\times10$. Since $\frac1{25} = 0.04$,
$$\frac1{62500} = 0.04\times0.04\times0.1\times0.1 = 0.000016.$$
There are 6 digits after the decimal point.

**Answer: (C) 6**

prism-2014-junior-09.title: Make the denominator a power of 10
prism-2014-junior-09.body:
$62500 = 2^2\times5^6$. Multiply top and bottom by $2^4$ to get $10^6$ underneath:
$$\frac1{62500} = \frac{16}{1\,000\,000} = 0.000016.$$
The last digit 6 is in the sixth decimal place.

**Answer: (C) 6**

prism-2014-junior-10.title: Each digit in each place twice
prism-2014-junior-10.body:
Of the 6 arrangements, each digit appears in each position exactly twice. So each column adds to $2(1+2+3) = 12$, and the total is $12\times(100 + 10 + 1) = 12\times111 = 1332$.

**Answer: (D) 1332**

prism-2014-junior-11.title: Eliminate $x$
prism-2014-junior-11.body:
Subtract the second equation from the first: $y = 0$. Then $4x = 4$, so $x = 1$. There is exactly one solution, $(1, 0)$.

**Answer: (B) 1**

prism-2014-junior-11.title: Two lines
prism-2014-junior-11.body:
The equations are lines with slopes $-\frac43$ and $-2$. Lines with different slopes cross at exactly one point (here $(1,0)$, which lies on both).

**Answer: (B) 1**

prism-2014-junior-12.title: Write an equation
prism-2014-junior-12.body:
Let a sweater cost $x$ and a shirt $y$ euro. Then $12x + 8y = 8x + 12y + 20$, so $4x - 4y = 20$ and $x - y = 5$. A sweater costs €5 more than a shirt.

**Answer: (D)**

prism-2014-junior-12.title: Cancel the common part
prism-2014-junior-12.body:
Both bundles contain 8 sweaters and 8 shirts. Removing those, the comparison becomes: 4 sweaters cost €20 more than 4 shirts. So each sweater costs €5 more than each shirt.

**Answer: (D)**

prism-2014-junior-13.title: Venn diagram
prism-2014-junior-13.body:
Males not from Galway: $40 - 20 = 20$. Galway students who are not male: $50 - 20 = 30$. Male Galway students: 20. That accounts for $20 + 30 + 20 = 70$ students, i.e. everyone, so 0 are left over.

**Answer: (A) 0**

prism-2014-junior-14.title: Total distance over total time
prism-2014-junior-14.body:
Let the hill be $d$ km. Up takes $\frac d{30}$ h, down $\frac d{45}$ h. Total time $\frac{3d + 2d}{90} = \frac{d}{18}$ h for a distance $2d$, so the average speed is $2d \div \frac d{18} = 36$ km/h.

**Answer: (D) 36**

prism-2014-junior-14.title: Pick a distance
prism-2014-junior-14.body:
Take the hill to be 90 km (a multiple of 30 and 45). Up: 3 hours; down: 2 hours. 180 km in 5 hours is 36 km/h. (Not the ordinary average 37.5 — the car spends longer at the slower speed.)

**Answer: (D) 36**

prism-2014-junior-15.title: Gauss's trick
prism-2014-junior-15.body:
Write $T = 1 + 2 + \cdots + 64$ forwards and backwards and add: each of the 64 pairs $1 + 64$, $2 + 63$, … sums to 65, so $2T = 64\times65$ and $T = 32\times65 = 2080$.

**Answer: (A) 2080**

prism-2014-junior-15.title: Formula
prism-2014-junior-15.body:
$1 + 2 + \cdots + n = \frac{n(n+1)}2$, so the total is $\frac{64\times65}{2} = 2080$ cents.

**Answer: (A) 2080**

prism-2014-junior-16.title: Speed ratios
prism-2014-junior-16.body:
When Andrew finishes 1000 m, Brian has run 800 m, so Brian runs at $\frac{800}{1000} = 80\%$ of Andrew's speed. Likewise Charlie runs at 80% of Brian's speed, i.e. $0.8\times0.8 = 64\%$ of Andrew's. When Andrew finishes, Charlie has run 640 m, so Andrew wins by $1000 - 640 = 360$ m.

**Answer: (C) 360**

prism-2014-junior-16.title: Follow Brian
prism-2014-junior-16.body:
When Andrew finishes, Brian is at 800 m. Brian beats Charlie by 200 m over 1000 m, so Charlie covers $\frac{800}{1000}$ of whatever Brian covers. While Brian runs 800 m, Charlie runs $800\times0.8 = 640$ m. Margin: $360$ m (not 400, a common trap).

**Answer: (C) 360**

prism-2014-junior-17.title: Find $c$
prism-2014-junior-17.body:
Dividing, $\frac{ac}{ab} = \frac{18}6$ gives $c = 3b$. Then $bc = 3b^2 = 27$, so $b = 3$, $c = 9$ and $a = 6\div3 = 2$. So $abc = 2\times3\times9 = 54$.

**Answer: (B) 54**

prism-2014-junior-18.title: Compute each
prism-2014-junior-18.body:
(A) $4\times5 = 20$. (B) side $x$ with $x^2 + x^2 = 50$, so $x = 5$ and perimeter 20. (C) side $\sqrt{25} = 5$, perimeter 20. (D) $2\pi\times3.5 = 7\pi \approx 22$. (E) $\pi r^2 = 9\pi$ gives $r = 3$, perimeter $6\pi \approx 18.8$. The largest is (D).

**Answer: (D)**

prism-2014-junior-18.title: Compare with 20
prism-2014-junior-18.body:
The three squares all have side 5, so perimeter 20. Since $\pi > 3$, the circle in (D) has perimeter $7\pi > 21 > 20$. The circle in (E) has radius 3, smaller than in (D), so it is smaller too.

**Answer: (D)**

prism-2014-junior-19.title: Pythagoras
prism-2014-junior-19.body:
Let the side be $x$ cm. The diagonal squared is $x^2 + x^2 = 2x^2$, and four times the perimeter is $16x$. So $2x^2 = 16x$, giving $x = 8$. The area is $8^2 = 64$ cm$^2$.

**Answer: (A) 64**

prism-2014-junior-19.title: Diagonal squared is twice the area
prism-2014-junior-19.body:
The square of the diagonal is always twice the area: $d^2 = 2A$. So $2A = 4\times4x$, i.e. $A = 8x$. But also $A = x^2$, so $x = 8$ and $A = 64$.

**Answer: (A) 64**

prism-2014-junior-20.title: Average of the raises
prism-2014-junior-20.body:
The average rises by the average raise: $\frac{3m + 1\cdot(n - m)}{n} = \frac{2m + n}{n} = 2\frac mn + 1$. Setting this equal to 1.5 gives $2\frac mn = 0.5$, so $\frac mn = \frac14$.

**Answer: (B) $\frac14$**

prism-2014-junior-20.title: Try a class of 4
prism-2014-junior-20.body:
Everyone gets at least 1 extra mark, so the extra 0.5 on average must come from the bonus 2 marks some students get. If a fraction $p$ of the class gets the bonus, the average goes up by $2p$ beyond 1, so $2p = 0.5$, $p = \frac14$. Check with 4 students, one raised by 3: total raise $3 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 6$, average $1.5$ ✔.

**Answer: (B) $\frac14$**
